Title: [from] Stardust
Author: by Shirley Anne Ramaley
Content: Have you ever seen a shooting star? They aren’t really stars at all. Shooting stars are meteors. They occur when a small chunk of debris burns up as it passes through the `text(Earth’s)` atmosphere.

The debris is called a meteoroid. It’s a very small piece of material. In fact, most are the size of dust particles. Others might be as big as baseballs. When a meteoroid burns up in the atmosphere, it is called a meteor or shooting star. It is the flash of light we see in the night sky.

If you lie on a blanket on a dark, moonless night and look up into the sky, you might spot brief streaks of light, shooting stars. They can be seen on any night that is clear and dark. Shooting stars are easier to see away from the city’s bright lights, but you can often see them if you’re in the city too.

Most shooting stars are left over material from a comet. As comets orbit the sun, they leave a stream of debris or material sbehind them. Because scientists can predict when `text(Earth)` will pass through the orbit of a comet, we know ahead of time when we can see meteor showers.

At certain times of the `text(year)`, meteor showers occur when the `text(Earth)` passes through the trail of debris left by a comet. At those times, the streaks of light are often seen every few `text(minutes)`. It’s quite a display in the night sky!

While most of us will see shooting stars, comets are harder to see and not as common. But there are comets you can see with the “naked eye,” without binoculars or a telescope. Once a comet is visible, it will look like a bright spot in the clear sky at night. It can be seen for `text(days)` and maybe `text(weeks)`. Then it will fade away and might not return for `text(thousands of years)`.
